extracted.intended_audience: readers, artists, and critics seeking criteria to judge what constitutes true art
extracted.subtask_description: Provide criteria for distinguishing real art from counterfeit art and for judging artistic merit across media, focusing on the transmission (infection) of feeling and on subject-matter judged by social/religious purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: art as transmission of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a human activity by means of which some people transmit their feelings to others (and not a service of Beauty, nor a manifestation of the Idea, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational definition used throughout: art's purpose is communicative—to infect others with the author's felt state. Anything that does not transmit feeling in this way is not art but a counterfeit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness (contagion of feeling) — the primary sign of real art
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one indubitable indication distinguishing real art from its counterfeit, namely, the infectiousness of art: if a man, without exercising effort and without altering his standpoint, on reading, hearing, or seeing another man’s work, experiences a mental condition which unites him with that man and with other people who also partake of that work of art, then the object evoking that condition is a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an internal, first-person sign (the feeling of union with the artist and with others). Examples: the author being moved by peasant women's singing or a simple child's tale which transmits feeling; contrasted with mere divertissement or excitement produced by counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of infectiousness as sole measure of excellence (as art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stronger the infection the better is the art, as art—speaking now apart from its subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging purely 'as art' (ignoring moral or subject-matter questions), use the strength of the transmitted feeling as the primary metric. Novelty, technical effects, or complexity do not substitute for degree of infection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality of the feeling transmitted
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three conditions determining infectiousness: the greater or lesser individuality of the feeling transmitted — the more individual the feeling transmitted the more strongly does it act on the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuality means the feeling comes from the artist's unique nature (not generic or borrowed). Highly individual states of soul give greater pleasure and stronger union in receivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three conditions determining infectiousness: the greater or lesser clearness with which the feeling is transmitted — clearness of expression assists infection because the receiver is better satisfied the more clearly the feeling is transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even an individual feeling will fail to infect if expressed obscurely. Clearness does not mean simplicity of subject-matter alone, but intelligibility of the felt state to the receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (inner need to express) — the decisive condition
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three conditions and the most important: the sincerity of the artist, i.e., the greater or lesser force with which the artist himself feels the emotion he transmits. The three conditions may all be summed up into one, the last, sincerity—that the artist should be impelled by an inner need to express his feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the spectator feels the artist is 'writing, singing, or playing for himself' and not 'doing it for' the receiver, infection follows. Conversely, art produced for vanity, covetousness, or to act upon others usually repels. Peasant art typically exemplifies sincerity; much upper-class art lacks it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence/presence rule for the three conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of infectiousness of art depends on individuality, clearness, and sincerity; the absence of any one of these conditions excludes a work from the category of art and relegates it to that of art’s counterfeits. If all these conditions are present, even in the smallest degree, then the work, even if weak, is yet a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by which of the three conditions they fulfil and to what degree. Different works may trade off (e.g., high individuality but less clearness), and merit is decided by the combination and degree of these three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter judged by contribution to human progress (religious perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, like speech, is a means of communication and therefore of progress—art renders accessible feelings needed for mankind’s well-being. The appraisement of feelings (i.e., which feelings are good or bad subject-matter) is made by the religious perception of the age: art is better insofar as its subject-matter furthers the movement of humanity toward perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good or bad subject-matter should be judged by whether the feelings it transmits make the religious perception of the age operative in life (i.e., promote kinder, more necessary feelings). Historical examples: Greek art choosing strength/courage; Jewish art choosing devotion/submission. Critics who deny religion may still implicitly appeal to a religious perception when appraising art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeit-art characteristics: borrowings, imitation, effects, interestingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeits of art are characterized by borrowings, imitation, effects, and interestingness replacing the contagion of feeling. These external devices counterfeit art and produce mere divertissement or hypnotic enchantment rather than genuine infection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and anti-patterns: Wagner’s operas (use of poetical arsenal, imitative sounds, striking stage effects, leit-motifs, novel dissonances, Bayreuth staging) are cited as model counterfeit art which uses hypnotic methods (darkness, invisible orchestra, repeated exposure) to enchant audiences. Beware productions that rely on novelty, sensory spectacle, or intellectual puzzles rather than transmitted feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: External technical perfection/staging is not proof of art
rubrics_metrics.description: The external quality of false productions is often no worse and often better than in real ones; the counterfeit is often more effective than the real and its subject more interesting. External perfection therefore does not guarantee art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate well-trained actors, elaborate mounting, perfect technique, or ornate decoration with true art—these can deceive and pervert taste. Compare, for instance, grand cathedral paintings produced for pay (criticized as imitations) versus modest works that truly transmit feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production intent and motive as evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the artist creates from an inner need (sincerity) or from aims of covetousness, vanity, or to act on others determines whether the work is art or counterfeit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the creator’s motive: works produced primarily for fame, money, or to impress (e.g., to be 'advanced and enlightened' by society) are likely counterfeit. Genuine art issues from private need and personal infection; public-minded or market-minded creation is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity: even small works with any degree of real conditions are art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the three conditions (individuality, clearness, sincerity) are present even in the smallest degree, then the work, though weak, is yet a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule prevents overly rigid exclusion: minor or simple works (folk-song, a child’s story, a drawing) that genuinely transmit feeling count as art. Evaluate on presence rather than scale of fulfilment.
